newsitem.title: USA: New York lawmaker seeks hurricane insurance fund.
newsitem.headline: New York lawmaker seeks hurricane insurance fund.

text.p: A New York state senator has introduced legislation to set up an insurer-financed catastrophe fund to pay homeowners' claims in the event of a hurricane, his aide said on Monday.
The proposal by state Sen. Guy Velella seeks to establish a pool for paying hurricane claims before a big storm strikes.

Velella, the Republican chairman of the Senate Insurance Committee and the Senate Majority Task Force on Catastrophe Insurance, made the proposal in late February, his aide Steve Casscles told Reuters.
Casscles said the fund's structure would be similar to that of a 401k plan, except it would be used to pay storm claims instead of provide retirement income.
The fund would be financed mainly by insurers with large exposures in New York's coastal areas, particularly in residential sections of Long Island and Staten Island, Casscles said.
He said insurers with large exposures included Allstate Corp, State Farm and Nationwide Insurance.
Velella introduced two catastrophe fund bills based on similar programs in Florida, the aide said.
Under one bill, state agencies would manage the fund. The other calls for an independent authority, which would ensure the state could not raid the fund for other purposes.

Casscles said the insurance committee had so far received mixed feedback from insurers. "There's a fear that we're shifting exposure from the big companies that are overexposed, like Allstate and State Farm, to smaller companies that do not create the problem," he said.
He said such fear was unfounded because each company would actually pay a premium based on its own exposure.

He said big insurers with heavy exposures "like the idea of some kind of cat fund, but they want it done in such a way that will shift the exposure from them to other companies -- and we do not want that to occur."

"The whole idea is that the money is available quickly so that they can pay off claims quickly. ...The benefit to the company is that right now there's no vehicle for them to put tax-deferred money into a fund."
